cells.tense: You're here with your hand on it — the schedule answers to you, not the other way around.
cells.ask: Pick the one thing you'll tend this week, turn down the second, and write down what each choice gives you by Friday.
cells.core:
Two things stay both alive in your hands right now — a person and a piece of work — and neither one goes hungry while you're at the other. You're not splitting yourself down the middle and you're not setting either one down; you turn to each at the pace it actually asks for, and the care gets made new when you come back to it.

What's underneath is you choosing, not the calendar choosing for you. The footing holds because you're standing on it. Say out loud which one you'd set down if it ever came to that — and let someone hear the answer, even if the answer is neither yet.

cells.tense: You're already living in a version of this that hasn't arrived — steering by the schedule that could break tomorrow.
cells.ask: Before bed tonight, put a hard stop on one thing you've been tending past your own edge, and see whether it kept growing without you.
cells.core:
Somewhere ahead is the day the two things collide, and you've started living there already. You check, you adjust, you head it off — every hand on the wheel is stopping a problem that may not even come. Care that answers something has a rhythm to it; care that has nothing to answer just keeps running, and that's what's running you at three in the morning.

The cost is the plain middle of things — nothing gets to be ordinary, so nothing gets to be easy. Let one thing keep growing without your weight on it, and see what it holds on its own.

cells.tense: You're still standing where the last thing ended — facing a door that closed before you reached it.
cells.ask: Write down one small responsibility you can actually carry today — one place you'll show up, one thing you'll feed — and do only that.
cells.core:
At its ordinary best this is unremarkable: what's in front of you gets picked up, kept up, one thing at a time. It isn't that now. What's in front of you looks like more than you can pick up, so none of it gets picked up, and the room has gone quiet around the things that used to be looked after. That isn't weakness. It's strength with no current moving through it, and nothing small enough to stand on.

What brings it back isn't gripping harder — it's finishing one reachable thing and feeling it done. That feeling is what carries you back to the rest.

cells.tense: You're the one doing the carrying, and you describe it as though it were happening around you.
cells.ask: Tell one person today about one effort you've made that no one has seen, and let them say it back to you as a fact.
cells.core:
You show up. You keep the schedule, you check on the person, you carry the thing no one else would — and it's going well enough that no one has to ask about it. You tell it like the situation asked for it, as if your showing up were just what the day required. But the day depends on choices you make, and those choices haven't been said out loud, so the whole arrangement gets filed under things-as-they-are.

The strength is real and it costs you something, and that cost has been paid by one person only. Say one honest thing about what you've put in, and let someone hear it. Letting go of the thing belongs on your schedule, not anyone else's.

attempts.check: The unsupported claim in my draft: I write 'two things at once' as what the strong form of this card does — that is in the record's own words about stewardship ('stewarding both with grace'), so the cell is saying it as an act rather than as the person's history. The reader might reasonably say 'I'm not holding two things, I'm holding ten, and none of them are getting the care they need' — so the cell names the bend as care going slack rather than claiming life is busy. If my read is wrong about the first cell, the ask still gives something back — writing the next thing down strips it to what one day, one set of hands can carry — so it survives being wrong. The sentence that serves the writer more than the reader is the one about 'the asking has gone quiet,' which I've threatened to place in two cells and cut from each.
